Read IN FULL: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev/646bc8ac-afb6-41b4-8d24-dcbaf28144cd/scratchpad/turns_chunk07.txt

This file contains every user turn Marcel Navarro typed across ~34 Claude Code sessions while working as FED Lead on the Zimmermann PWA Kit (a Salesforce PWA Kit / React / Chakra codebase). Sessions are separated by `====` lines with a `### [tag] [date] Title — N user turns` header. Turns are marked `--- turn N ---`.

READ THE WHOLE FILE. It is large (~445,000 tokens), so read it in sequential slices using Read with offset/limit. Maintain a running findings list as you go and DISCARD raw text after each slice — never try to hold the whole file in context.

We are designing personal workflow skills for Marcel. The transcripts are the evidence for WHY those skills are needed. Extract these six things:

**1. RECURRING CORRECTIONS — the highest priority.**
Places where Marcel had to re-state an established way of working that had been ignored or got wrong. He has said he had to "stress again and again" the set approach. Find those. For each, give: verbatim quote (trimmed to the relevant sentences), the session title, turn number, and tag it with the area:
`overriding` | `tokens` | `components` | `atomic-design` (atoms/molecules/organisms) | `css-structure` | `css-strategy` | `tests` | `stories` | `a11y` | `typescript` | `contentful` | `scope` | `git/branching` | `other`
Count how many DISTINCT times each area comes up. That count is the single most important output.

**2. DESIGN CONFORMANCE.**
Where he had to check or re-check that a build matched the Figma design — variants, states, tokens, viewports, spacing. Quote the checks he actually performs and what he looks for.

**3. FRUSTRATION / RE-WORK SIGNALS.**
Turns containing corrections: "again", "I said", "no —", "that's not", "you missed", "why did you", "revert", "you were supposed to", "as I mentioned". These mark where the workflow broke down. Quote and categorise.

**4. WHAT WORKED.**
Successes. Especially any use of a closed-loop / multi-agent / orchestrator-builder-tester-scorer workflow. Quote how he set it up and what he said about the result. Also note any prompt pattern he reused because it worked.

**5. HIS PROMPT FORMULAS.**
Recurring phrasings and structures he types — the shape of his asks. We want to encode his voice and method into skills, so capture the actual language, not a paraphrase.

**6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR.**
He is also senior dev / reviewer. Where he reviews others' PRs or code, capture: what he checks, in what order, what he rejects, and how he phrases feedback.

OUTPUT: a structured report with these six sections. Lead section 1 with a frequency table of areas. Use verbatim quotes throughout — quotes are the deliverable, not summaries. Be concrete. If a section has nothing, say so explicitly.

1935	ELI5 but i'm the FED Lead:
1936	
1937	Found the likely root cause — and it's a real CI/CD gap, not a one-off fluke
1938	Two more findings that settle this:
1939	
1940	1. Not caching — the page request itself was `x-cache: Miss from cloudfront`, a genuine cache miss. The origin server itself is serving the old config; nothing is being served stale from a cache.
1941	2. The likely actual bug: `pwa-kit-dev push`'s own `--help` shows a `--wait` flag described as "wait for the deployment to complete before exiting." Our deploy script (`npm run push:dev` = `pwa-kit-dev push -t dev`) doesn't use `-w`/`--wait`. That means the CLI can report success the moment the bundle finishes uploading — without ever confirming the subsequent deploy-to-target step actually completed. That matches exactly what we're seeing: the log's last real line is `success: Bundle Uploaded`, not "deployed" — and the live site never actually got the new bundle activated. This is a plausible, well-supported explanation, not a certainty (I can't see MRT's own internal logs to prove it definitively).

1943	What needs to be done
1944	Tactical (fixes dev right now):

1946	* Re-run the same already-completed GitHub Action (`gh run rerun 31236585642`) — re-executes build+push against our merge commit. The workflow only triggers on `push` to develop (no manual `workflow_dispatch`), so re-running the existing run is the cleanest way to retry without a new commit.
1947	* Alternative: push a trivial commit to `develop` to naturally re-trigger it.

Implement the following plan:

# SFCC-89 — plan assurance pass (scaled-down closed loop)

**Planned 2026-08-25.** Verification only. No repo file changes.

---

## Context

The first closed loop — 8 invocations, 6 agent types, 1 revision round — produced a verified divergence register and a realignment plan. That plan has since been **edited roughly fifteen times**: Figma verification corrected the meta-block rhythm from 20px to 28px, the Jira ticket corrected the scope premise (six enumerated fields, a Contentful exclusion, a documented missing SFCC attribute), an over-delivery audit cut two items, a V&V pass reversed two of those cuts and found two new must-fix defects (D17 skeleton/CLS, D18 bundle price gate), and seven decisions were settled.

**Stages 5 and 6 verified revision 1. Nothing has verified the final plan.**

So the content is better than what the loop produced, and the coherence is less assured. That asymmetry is the whole reason for this pass.

**Specific unknowns:** the G2/G4 gate floors may have drifted (one test removed, several added) · whether D18's `price={isProductPartOfBundle ? undefined : info.price}` composes correctly through D1's optional prop and the atom's null-return · whether removing `useUiCopy` leaves anything dangling · whether the story trims break a cross-referencing assertion.

**Outcome wanted:** the plan restored to the verification standard the register already meets — not new findings for their own sake.

---

## Why this is 2 agents and not 8

The original loop's Stages 1–3 (rubric, #59 catalogue, our-code catalogue, register) ran against inputs that **have not changed**: the 29 files are untouched, #59 is merged and static, the `~/Dev` docs are static. Re-deriving them has a marginal find rate near zero.

Every blocker the first loop found came from the **plan-verification** stages. Those are exactly what's now stale. So this pass re-runs that half and nothing else.

The mechanism that produced confidence last time was **two independent agents on overlapping-but-distinct briefs converging on the same findings** — and a reconciler who checked source when they disagreed (which settled the nine-vs-three removal-list dispute). That is preserved. What's dropped is re-gathering unchanged facts.

## Three failure modes from the first loop, and the fix

| Failure | Fix in this pass |
|---|---|
| An agent scoped away from the evidence its question needed, and returned a confident wrong verdict (the `audit:tokens` baseline) | Both agents may read the `~/Dev` docs. The local-only constraint stays: never cite them by filename in anything repo-bound. |
| An agent given a wrong premise ("five enumerated fields") wasted its verdicts | Both agents get the **Jira scope verbatim**, not my summary of it. |
| Every pass still missed something — D17 survived eight invocations | Both briefs carry a **mandatory "what is missing" section**. Verifying stated claims is not sufficient output. |

---

## The pipeline

### Stage 0 — live gate re-run (me, before the agents)

Four read-only gates now, so the agents verify against measured numbers rather than stated ones:

`npx tsc --noEmit` · `npx vitest run` · `npm run lint` · `npm run audit:tokens`

`npm run build-storybook` writes to `storybook-static/`, so it is **not** runnable in plan mode — it moves to Stage 0 of execution. Current stated baselines to confirm or correct: tsc 0 · Vitest 354/22 · lint 17 errors / 16 warnings · audit:tokens 19 unacknowledged / 16 acknowledged.

### Stage 1 — two agents, parallel

**Agent A — coherence and traceability.** Does the plan hang together as a sequence?
- Every step traces to a register row, including the new D17 and D18.
- Each commit leaves the branch green; no step depends on a later one.
- The interaction questions above — D18 × D1 × optional prop; `useUiCopy` removal completeness; story trims against existing cross-referencing assertions.
- Any step contradicting another, or contradicting a settled decision.
- Any register row with no step and no explicit disposition.

**Agent B — feasibility and numbers.** Can it physically be executed, and are the figures right?
- **Predict the gate numbers at each commit** given the test and story changes — this is the drift question, and Stage 0's measurements are the baseline to reason from.
- Every named file, export, hook, token, recipe key and line citation exists.
- The prettier normalisation command in COMMIT 1's body actually produces the claimed diff.
- Tier and CODEOWNERS set still accurate; no Tier 1 path; no new package.
- Collisions with `f2r-component-registry` and SFCC-737.

Both: falsify rather than confirm · verdicts **CORRECT / WRONG (with what is true) / CONTESTED (with counter-evidence)** · do not re-litigate settled decisions, they are the developer's · read-only, no writes, no mutating git.

### Stage 2 — reconciliation (me)

Agree → accept. **Disagree → I check source myself**, which is what caught the last inter-agent dispute. Neither caught something I spot → add it.

**Auto-apply boundary.** Per your call, unambiguous corrections go straight into the artefacts. Narrowly defined, so it cannot swallow judgement:

| Auto-apply | Report first |
|---|---|
| A number a command output contradicts | Adding, removing or reordering a step |
| A `file:line` citation pointing at the wrong line | Changing what a step does |
| A named file/export/token that does not exist, where the correct name is unambiguous | Anything touching scope or a settled decision |
| Typos and stale cross-references | Anything the two agents disagree on |

Every auto-applied change is logged in a **Changelog** section at the foot of the realignment plan — nothing changes invisibly.

### Stage 3 — conditional, one targeted agent

Only if reconciliation surfaces something material that neither agent covered. One focused check, not a round. **Termination: one round.** Anything unresolved after Stage 3 escalates to you rather than looping.

---

## Critical inputs

`~/.claude/plans/sfcc-89-realignment-plan.md` (under test) · `~/.claude/plans/sfcc-89-realignment-register.md` (the evidence base) · `~/.claude/plans/sfcc-89-scope-reference.md` (owner table and locked decisions) · the Jira scope, supplied verbatim in each brief · the repo at `8362b3c` with 29 staged files · the three `~/Dev` docs, readable but never citable in repo-bound output.

**Do not re-derive:** the rubric, the #59 pattern catalogue, the our-code catalogue, or any register row already marked CONFIRMED. Those inputs are unchanged.

---

## Verification — how we know this pass is sound

1. **The two agents converge**, or every divergence is resolved by me against source, with the check recorded.
2. **Both "what is missing" sections are non-empty or explicitly reasoned as empty.** A verification pass that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable of finding anything.
3. **Stage 0's measured numbers appear in the corrected plan** — no gate figure survives that a command contradicts.
4. **The four open items and the settled decisions are still present and unaltered.** A pass that quietly drops one has optimised for tidiness.
5. **The Changelog lists every auto-applied change**, and I can point at the command output or line that justified each.

## What this pass buys, and what it does not

It restores the plan to the standard the register already meets, and it closes four named unknowns with measured numbers.

It does **not** guarantee nothing is missed — no pass in this sequence has, and D17 survived eight invocations before being found. Treat a clean result as "verified to the same standard as everything else here", not as proof.

## Then

===== ZEPHYR turn 1 (full)
# Zephyr Test Case Generation — Workflow
Save as `~/tools/zephyr/zephyr-workflow.md`.
Invoke with: `claude "Follow ~/tools/zephyr/zephyr-workflow.md for SFCC-1234"`
---
## Role
You generate Zephyr Scale test cases from Jira requirements and upload them as
**drafts for human review**. You are the first pass, not the final word. A QA
engineer reviews everything you produce in the Zephyr UI before it becomes real.
## Constants
| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Jira site | `zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net` |
| Project key | `SFCC` |
| Target folder | `/Staging/<JIRA-KEY>` |
| Status on write | `Draft` — never anything else |
| Upload script | `~/tools/zephyr/zephyr-upload.ts` |
| Token | `$ZEPHYR_TOKEN` from Keychain — never read, print, or log it |
---
## Procedure
### 1. Read the requirement
Via the Atlassian MCP, fetch the Jira issue: summary, description, acceptance
criteria, issue type, status, **and comments**. Requirements frequently live in
comments rather than the description — read them.
Follow every linked Confluence page and read it. If a link is dead or you lack
access, say so explicitly rather than proceeding on partial information.
### 2. Assess before generating
Report to the user, before writing anything:
- How many distinct acceptance criteria you found
- Anything ambiguous, contradictory, or underspecified
- Anything referenced but unreadable
**If acceptance criteria are ambiguous, stop and ask.** Do not resolve ambiguity
by picking the most plausible reading. A confidently-worded test case built on a
guess is worse than no test case, because it passes review by looking right.
### 3. Generate
One test case per acceptance criterion, plus error and edge paths **that the
requirement actually states**. Do not invent requirements to reach a target count.
Naming: `<Feature>: <behaviour being verified>`
e.g. `Checkout: rejects expired payment method`
Each case gets:
- `name` — as above, unique within the project
- `objective` — one sentence, what this proves
- `precondition` — required state, or omit
- `folder` — `/Staging/<JIRA-KEY>`
- `statusName` — `Draft`
- `priorityName` — inherit from the Jira issue priority
- `labels` — `["<JIRA-KEY>", "ai-generated", "needs-review"]`
- `linkedIssueKey` — the Jira key
- `steps` — each with `description` and `expectedResult`
**Steps must be executable by someone who has not read the ticket.** Concrete
values, named UI elements, observable outcomes. `expectedResult` states what the
tester can see, not what the system does internally.
Bad: `Verify the payment fails appropriately.`
Good: `Error banner reads "Card expired". Order status remains Pending. No charge appears in the payment log.`
### 4. Report coverage gaps
Before uploading, list what you could **not** test from the requirement as
written — unstated error paths, missing edge cases, integration points the
ticket doesn't describe.
This section is the point of the exercise. You can only test what the ticket
says; the gaps are where the QA engineer's domain knowledge is needed. Surface
them as a list for the reviewer to act on. Never fill them in yourself.
### 5. Write and confirm
Write the JSON to `/tmp/zephyr-<JIRA-KEY>.json` and show the user a summary:
case count, names, folder, gap list.
**Wait for explicit approval before uploading.** Do not chain step 6.
### 6. Upload

```bash
cd ~/tools/zephyr && npx tsx zephyr-upload.ts /tmp/zephyr-<JIRA-KEY>.json
```

Run `--dry-run` first if the flag exists. Report per-case success or failure with
the returned Zephyr keys. Do not retry failures automatically — report and stop.
### 7. Hand off
Output for the reviewer:
- Zephyr folder path and the test case keys created
- Case count
- The coverage gap list from step 4
- Anything you flagged as ambiguous in step 2
---
## Hard constraints
- **Write only to `/Staging/<JIRA-KEY>`.** Never to any other folder.
- **Status is always `Draft`.** You never mark anything `Approved`. Approval is a
  human act performed in the Zephyr UI.
- **Never modify or delete existing test cases** outside `/Staging`. If a case
  with the same name exists elsewhere, report the collision and stop.
- **Never delete anything** in Zephyr under any circumstances.
- **Never print the token**, in output, logs, or error messages.
- **Never invent requirements.** If the ticket doesn't say it, it goes in the gap
  list, not in a test case.
- **Never batch multiple Jira issues** in one run without being asked.
## Re-running
Re-running for the same Jira key is safe: the script matches on name and
overwrites steps rather than appending. Cases the reviewer already moved out of
`/Staging` will not be touched — they are outside your write scope, so a re-run
regenerates only what is still in staging.
If the requirement changed, say so in the handoff so the reviewer knows which
cases are newly stale.

===== Contentful v PWA Kit turn 3 (meeting 2 notes)
meeting 2 notes:

"Based on the transcribed meeting discussion.
FED Executive Takeaway
The strongest message from Tim was:
Stop thinking about pages as primary deliverables and think about reusable, configurable components as the primary deliverables.
The homepage, cart, PDP/PLP experiences, etc. should largely become assemblies of previously built components, not separate frontend implementations.
For FED, this means:
Component completeness is critical.
Variant support must be designed upfront.
Contentful configuration drives rendering.
Page stories should primarily validate composition and integration, not rebuild functionality.
What Matters Most for FED
1. Components Must Support All Variants
The editorial card example was used repeatedly.
The expectation is that a FED developer building a component should account for:
text alignment variants
CTA visibility variants
title visibility variants
body copy variants
layout variants
before the component is considered complete.
FED Implication
Avoid:
Homepage Editorial Card
PLP Editorial Card
Landing Page Editorial Card
Instead:
One Editorial Card component + all supported variants
The page determines configuration.
The component owns behavior.
2. FED Stories Should Focus on Rendering Behavior
There was a clear separation made between:
Contentful Stories
Responsible for:
content model fields
editorial configuration
required/optional fields
authoring controls
FED / PWA Stories
Responsible for:
rendering
responsiveness
accessibility
link behavior
user interactions
component state handling
This is actually useful from a backlog standpoint because it removes duplication between Contentful and FED work.
Potential FED Story Pattern
Instead of:
Build Editorial Card
Think:
Render Editorial Card content model according to Figma specifications across all supported configurations.
3. Accessibility Requirements Need To Be Explicit
One specific implementation point surfaced.
For image alt text:
If alt text exists → render it.
If alt text does not exist → do not render the attribute.
For FED this means:
accessibility behavior should be documented directly in ACs
don't assume CMS fields are always populated
frontend rendering needs to account for missing content safely
4. Homepage Tickets Are Probably Over-Scoped
A major discussion point was:
"What actually belongs in a Homepage Epic?"
The consensus was essentially:
The homepage is mostly:
Hero
Editorial modules
Category modules
Content modules
Promotional modules
all assembled together.
If those components already exist, there shouldn't be significant additional frontend implementation.
FED Impact
When sizing homepage work:
Separate:
Component Build
real FED effort
from
Page Composition
assembly/configuration effort
integration testing
visual validation
Those should not be estimated the same way.
5. Component Validation Should Happen Early
Tim described an iterative approach where components are progressively dropped into a working homepage as they're completed.
Rather than:
Build everything
Then build homepage
Then test homepage
the idea is:
Build component
Drop component into page
Verify rendering
Repeat
FED Impact
This aligns well with:
Storybook
Preview environments
Contentful preview workflows
Incremental QA
Potentially less big-bang integration risk later.
6. Page-Level Testing Still Belongs To FED
Even though pages aren't primary development units anymore, the meeting did reinforce that pages still need validation.
Specifically:
spacing
layout
design fidelity
responsive behavior
assembled user experience
Once the page is composed, someone still needs to verify that it matches design expectations.
FED Ownership Area
I would expect FED to remain heavily involved in:
visual QA
responsive QA
integration validation
design parity verification
even if the page itself isn't a dedicated implementation story.
Areas Where FED Should Push Back / Ask Questions
Recommendation Components
The cart example exposed some unclear requirements around:
Recommended For You
Shop The Look
Complete The Look
Questions raised included:
Manual curation?
Product relationships?
Behavioural/personalized recommendations?
Cookie-dependent experiences?
The group did not resolve this.
FED Risk
Frontend implementation differs significantly depending on:
static curated content
SFCC-driven recommendations
Einstein recommendations
personalization engines
Before sizing work, FED should ensure ownership and data source are clarified.
External Link Handling
There was uncertainty around:
external links
opening new tabs
security-related link attributes
No final decision was reached.
FED Follow-Up Needed
Before component implementation begins, confirm the desired standard for:
external links
internal links
new-tab behavior
Otherwise multiple developers may implement differently.
Contentful + FED Architecture Alignment
One of the most important architectural statements from the meeting was Tim's rule:
If the content doesn't come from a product or category source, it likely belongs in Contentful.
For FED, this provides a simple mental model:
Content Source	Likely OwnerProduct data	SFCC
Category data	SFCC
Merchandising content	Contentful
Marketing content	Contentful
Editorial content	Contentful
Promotional messaging	Contentful
This should help when evaluating future component requirements and determining where props/data should originate.
What I Would Take Back as FED Lead
Backlog / Delivery
Continue pushing component-first delivery.
Avoid page-specific component duplication.
Ensure every component story explicitly includes variants.
Technical
Define a standard renderer contract between Contentful models and React components.
Ensure components gracefully handle optional fields.
Document accessibility expectations component-by-component.
Risk Areas
Recommendation engines/content source still unclear.
External-link implementation still unresolved.
Some merchandising journeys need business clarification before development sizing.
Overall Assessment"

## 4. WHAT WORKED

### 4a. The closed-loop multi-agent workflow — his own invention, stated verbatim

This is the single highest-value artefact in the corpus. He *designed* it in one turn:

> "for the execution and build on this let's utilize a **'workflow improvement closed-loop agent workflow'**:
> - an **orchestrator agent** that oversees the entire process while also doubling as a **scope checker to ensure we are delivering fully to spec - not under or over**,
> - a **builder / implementer agent** that executes the plan,
> - a **tester agent** that tests the work and output by deploying different subagents to check across the different aspects and angles that the build must pass,
> - a **scorer agent** that checks the code, the output, and the results from the tester agent and scores by checking the quality and either marks the work as complete or **returns the work to the implementer to improve and then back to the tester agent and so on until it's marked as passed**
> - and lastly **an agent that listens to and tracks the entire flow on the loop and takes note for improvement that is applied to the orchestrator, builder/implementer, tester, and scorer agents while the loop continues to run**
>
> this is to achieve the /goal to build this user story **as prescribed by the user story / ticket, as designed in figma, as intended to be approached by the docs and as established in PR #59** which is now in develop and is also the base of this working branch, and lastly **using the token, components, css structure, and overriding approach (as appropriately)**"
> — *SFCC - PR #57, turn 31*

**It ran and it worked.** The loop executed across five commits with visible Builder → Tester → Builder-rework → Scorer → Retrospective cycles (turns 34–81), including two rework rounds on COMMIT 1 alone. His own verdict on the process:

> "overall **i think it went well**, from information gathering to running the review to executing the comments, amidst the oversights here and there"
> — *ZIMM - PR #68 (2), turn 27*

And he asked for a written rundown of it at the end, i.e. he wanted it captured as reusable:
> "give me a rundown of the closed-loop multi-agent workflow that we did for the PDP Static work" — *SFCC - PR #57, turn 126*

**He reused it three more times** after inventing it:
> "execute a **closed-loop multi-agent workflow** to review this PR but **scaled appropriately to the need**, nothing too crazy/too much and most definitely no overthinking, **you already know what to do ;)**" — *ZIMM - PR #68 (2), turn 3*
> "let's run an in-depth check and audit **via a closed-loop multi-agent workflow** into the PR itself, the findings we've found, and the fixes made for it" — *ZIMM - PR #68 (2), turn 27*
> "…**via closed-loop multi-agent**" *(appended to a three-item check list)* — *SFCC - PR #57, turn 83*

The `you already know what to do ;)` is the tell — by 29 Aug the loop had become a named, assumed-shared protocol.

### 4b. The "plan assurance pass" — a scaled-down loop applied to a *plan*, not code

He accepted a full plan (PR #57 turn 1) that encodes several reusable mechanisms:

> "The mechanism that produced confidence last time was **two independent agents on overlapping-but-distinct briefs converging on the same findings** — and a reconciler who checked source when they disagreed."
> "Both briefs carry a **mandatory 'what is missing' section**. Verifying stated claims is not sufficient output."
> "**Both agents get the Jira scope verbatim, not my summary of it.**"
> "**falsify rather than confirm** · verdicts **CORRECT / WRONG (with what is true) / CONTESTED (with counter-evidence)** · do not re-litigate settled decisions, **they are the developer's**"
> "**Auto-apply boundary**": auto-apply = "A number a command output contradicts / A `file:line` citation pointing at the wrong line / A named file/export/token that does not exist / Typos"; report-first = "Adding, removing or reordering a step / Changing what a step does / Anything touching scope or a settled decision / **Anything the two agents disagree on**"
> "**Termination: one round.** Anything unresolved after Stage 3 escalates to you rather than looping."
> "**A verification pass that finds nothing has not been shown to be capable of finding anything.**"
> — *SFCC - PR #57, turn 1*

That last line and the one-round termination rule are the direct antidote to his #2 frustration ("going back and forth with executing V&Vs… triggers a sense of uncertainty and mistrust").

### 4c. Gates as named, numbered pass criteria (G1–G7)

The loop used named gates he referred to conversationally: "G6 - looks exactly as the base pdp", "G6 pass, start commit 5", "what's needed for G6?", "Re-run G7 after rework". G4 = Storybook rendered output; G6 = his own manual visual check; G7 = a background command. Having a *number* he could pass/fail is what let him gate progress ("go, start commit 4").

### Two things a skill design should not miss

1. **The five-item approach list (`overriding · tokens · components · file/css structuring · scope`) is the thing he re-states most.** It should be a preamble the agent loads automatically, not something he types.
2. **His two named workflows already exist and worked** — the orchestrator/builder/tester/scorer/tracker loop (PR #57 t31) and the two-agent plan-assurance pass with its auto-apply boundary and one-round termination (PR #57 t1). The second one exists specifically to stop the failure he named in SFCC-237 t72 ("back and forth with executing V&Vs… triggers a sense of uncertainty and mistrust"). Encoding those two verbatim is higher value than inventing anything new.
